headline: TransDigm: sales up 23% with 14% organic growth and a 53% EBITDA margin; 2027 guidance points to adjusted EPS of about $47.50
takeaway: Fourth-quarter sales rose 23% to $3.0 billion, organic growth was 14% and adjusted EPS rose 15% to $12.44, ahead of the $12.21 consensus. TransDigm guided to 2027 adjusted EPS of $47.09–$47.94, up 15%, after a year in which it spent $4.4 billion on acquisitions and $2.8 billion on buybacks.
results: TransDigm reported net sales of $2,988 million for the quarter ended September 30, up 23%, with organic growth of 14% and the rest from acquisitions. EBITDA As Defined rose 20% to $1,583 million, a margin of 53.0% that includes about two points of dilution from recently acquired businesses. Adjusted EPS was $12.44, up 15%; GAAP EPS rose 33% to $10.33, although net income fell 4% to $586 million because of higher interest and tax costs.

For fiscal 2026 sales rose 20% to $10.6 billion, with 11% organic growth (13% excluding non-aerospace sales), and the EBITDA As Defined margin was 52.7%. The company bought Simmonds Precision Products, Jet Parts Engineering, Victor Sierra Aviation and Prince & Izant — the last for about $1.07 billion in September — plus twelve smaller businesses.

TransDigm repurchased 820,000 shares for $943 million in the quarter at an average of $1,150, and $2.8 billion for the year. It issued $3.0 billion of 6.75% secured notes due 2035 and used most of the proceeds to retire notes due 2028.
mgmt: Chief executive Mike Lisman said fourth-quarter results exceeded the high end of guidance for both revenue and EBITDA As Defined, that more than $7 billion was deployed in fiscal 2026 through acquisitions and buybacks, and that the company enters 2027 with significant liquidity and flexibility for more deals.

For fiscal 2027 TransDigm expects sales of $11.95 billion to $12.15 billion, up 14% at the midpoint; EBITDA As Defined of $6.20 billion to $6.35 billion, a margin of about 52%; GAAP EPS of $42.06 to $42.91; and adjusted EPS of $47.09 to $47.94, up 15%. Management said all three end markets — commercial aftermarket, commercial original equipment and defence — are positioned for growth.
view: TransDigm is one of the most unusual business models in the stock market. It buys makers of small, often sole-source aircraft parts — valves, sensors, actuators — whose cost is trivial relative to the aircraft but whose failure is not, then raises prices relentlessly, especially on spare parts sold to airlines. The result is an EBITDA margin above 50%, a level more typical of software than of manufacturing, and a company that funds its growth with borrowed money because the cash flows are so predictable.

This quarter showed the machine running at full speed. Organic growth of 14% reflects record air travel, ageing fleets kept flying longer because Boeing and Airbus cannot deliver new aircraft fast enough, and rising defence budgets. The margin slipped only because newly acquired businesses have not yet been put through TransDigm’s pricing and cost playbook — which, judging by history, means they will be. The 2027 guidance of 14% sales growth and a flat margin is typically conservative.

The risks are leverage and politics. TransDigm carries about $34 billion of debt, refinances constantly and pays special dividends funded partly by borrowing; higher rates, which drove net income down 4% this quarter, are its natural enemy. Its pricing also draws periodic scrutiny from the Pentagon and Congress. And with the shares around 24 times next year’s adjusted earnings, investors are paying for continued double-digit compounding. The record says that is a reasonable bet; this report adds to the record.
watch: Watch commercial aftermarket growth as airline traffic normalises, the margin progress at Simmonds and the other 2026 acquisitions, and whether TransDigm announces another special dividend or a large deal with its liquidity.
